commentBody: This was the rare puzzle that I solved 36% faster than my Saturday average, but I kept feeling I was going to get stuck on until the last letter was in.
Not sure why Caitlin thought this one was so hard. I solved it in 9:45, well under my Saturday average. Perhaps the constructor and I were just on the same wavelength.
I had about three squares I wasn't sure of, and had to keep trying different letters until I hit the music. Did not expect that CAR would cross CAR.
TILSIT crossing with MITES is pretty cruel... MOTES seems like the more apt answer for a tiny piece of something.
Editing is a thankless job, but I think the clues the editors rejected were good decision in this case, as those clues were a little *too* cute.

Phew!  That was a tough one because there was so much general knowledge/trivia.  (I expect a flood of complaints). I might still be struggling, but for the fact that I had read Under The Volcano many years ago, which gave me DIADELOSMUERTOS.  For anyone not familiar with the book, it’s beautifully written, but unrelentingly depressing.  Perhaps my view of it is clouded by the fact that I read it when I was going through a very rough patch in my life and I identified too closely with the protagonist. Despite getting that initial grid spanner, I fumbled around in other parts of the puzzle, especially the SE: the GABE OBELI cross nearly did me in.  Having completed it I reached the ex post facto conclusion that I enjoyed it immensely

Weird to see KAMASUTRA two days in a row — yesterday’s clue was better.

Precipitously for RAINY, on the other hand, was a nice touch.

My last to fall was RAINY for [Precipitous?] My mind went to a precipice/cliff, and then went to something done suddenly and rashly. Finally precipitation came to me with a big head slap. GARGANTUA popped into my mind out of nowhere, with just the initial G and final A in place. The things we remember and don't realize we remember until given two letters... And I took a shot at DYSPhorIA knowing full well it was wrong before DYSPEPSIA came to me (because Pepcid AC...) The puzzle was a nice brain workout because of the cluing – one of those that I thought I'd be up a creek without a paddle trying to solve, but that surprised me with the simplicity of the entries once they were gotten. Very nicely done, Mr. Levy. Thank you! (And here now, my favorite song from Pearl Jam's TEN album: https://youtu.be/n3r9KWth84Y?is=v9b3W9DV_f2I600b) It's worth saying that Eddie Vedder's diction is impenetrable, so if you'd like to know what on earth he's singing, watch this: https://youtu.be/oO6wPWFMrCA?is=VBw4HDUo2gWyTh9S 😜😂

TILSIT... OMG! I finally  realized what was going on here. I mean, I had been very surprised that there seemed to be a European cheese I was not familiar with. But I *did* know it - sadly only under the Polish name of "ser tylżycki" - Tylża is the Polish name for Tilsit. Historically it was an important place for us Poles, as in 1807 a treaty was signed there that led to the creation of Księstwo Warszawskie, the Duchy of Warsaw. At the time Poland had been partitioned by Russia, Prussia and Austria for more than a decade - it had ceased to exist as an independent state in 1795. The Napoleon-aligned Duchy of Warsaw was perceived as a resurrected Poland, and allied with an unstoppable conqueror, too - people had high hopes for the future, dreaming of Poland becoming the successor to Russia as Eastern Europe's superpower. Soon though everything came crashing down with the disastrous Russian campaign of 1812...

Who knew a quite unspectacular cheese could inspire a history lesson?

A tale of two puzzles for me.

Top half, a beget-fest.  Where you start with little islands in a sea of white, and suddenly from crosses, or maybe the brain taps your shoulder because it just cracked a clue, an answer that stumped you moments before, hits you.  That answer trips off another, which begets another, and in what feels like a wham, an expanse is filled, and you are thrilled.

Bottom half, a trek.  Those islands remain stubborn.  You return to them and they stay tight lipped.  Where you really have to sweat, call in the reserves. Squares do eventually relinquish themselves, but begrudgingly.  You end up feeling accomplished, but you don’t want to think – about anything – for a while.

I love both scenarios -- work and play -- so got my money’s worth today. 

Along the way, I enjoyed the international feel, with BALI, DIA DE LOST MUERTOS, IRANIAN, REVERAS, CORONATION ROBES, RIGA, TILSIT, KAMA SUTRA, and CABOS.

Thus, a splendid outing for me.  Thank you, Zachary!

I guessed the answer must be Moria anyway, but couldn’t get the crosses to fit for a while.

I read Tolkien first circa 1969, about the time The Beatles Abbey Road came out.  First LP I ever saved up for and bought myself.  All the cool 6th graders loved Abbey Road, and I was trying to be cool too.  But the music transcended that stuff.  

Reading Tolkien was definitely uncool.  Until Led Zeppelin’s Ramble On penetrated our consciousness when we weren’t teeny boppers anymore.

The many underground scenes… goblin tunnels, Erebor, Moria… are indelibly linked with Come Together and She’s So Heavy in my memory.

But that Durin tomb… I blanked on the quotation itself… looking up now it is part of a poem/song in The Lord of the Rings.  As a kid I just skipped those.  Eventually I heard recordings of Tolkien himself… I think I bought his LP in the 1970s.

“… 
The world is grey, the mountains old,
The forge's fire is ashen-cold;
No harp is wrung, no hammer falls:
The darkness dwells in Durin's halls;
The shadow lies upon his tomb
In Moria, in Khazad-dûm.
But still the sunken stars appear
In dark and windless Mirrormere;
There lies his crown in water deep,
Till Durin wakes again from sleep”

No value judgments here, just an observation. 3. A certain rock band's abbreviated name/chess rating system hasn't appeared in the puzzle yet this year. If that holds through the end of the year - actually it is still early - it would break a streak that goes back to 1994. I miss seeing the band name as an answer from time-to time, they've been a favorite of mine for a looong time.

Here's a perfectly innocent inquiry of those who create crosswords.  I hereby declare the "I'm just asking questions" invincibility cloak.

We know you sometimes construct around a theme.  So you have a set of answers that you must get into your grid.

But for the rest, do you specifically look for words like "mites" and "motes" that can be clued indistinguishably?

And for MOIL and TOIL?  Also, from previous puzzles SAPOR and SAVOR.  There are a lot of examples.  Every bitter commenter (unlike my perfect self) has their pet example.

It's perfectly fine if you do, but I'm curious if such sadism inflicted on the solver is intentional or not.
